For some, "**strong** confirmation" might seem like it's worded too strongly, but by saying there is a *remarkable* correlation, the author is saying, "It's an incredibly tight fit between prediction and data. This is a pretty compelling sign that we're on the right track."

choices.text: reveals that the earth's magnetic reversals have occurred at very regular intervals
choices.tag: Out of Scope: very regular intervals
choices.explanation:
At no point in the passage are we told that the polarity reversals occur at *very regular* intervals (i.e. "once every 100,000 years").

We're only told that scientists have assigned ages to the reversals, but those periods between reversals might vary a lot in length.

Maybe it reverses 1 million years ago, reverses back 200,000 years later, reverses back 50,000 years later, reverses back 350,000 years later, etc.

We're never told that the striping pattern consists of same-sized stripes. There could be a thick stripe followed by a thin stripe followed by a medium stripe, etc.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of magnetite grains?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: In molten magma, magnetite grains align with Earths magnetic field. Cooling locks in that alignment, recording the fields polarity then. Paragraph 3 directly states that the youngest rocks have normal polarity, meaning alignment with the present field. Keep magnetic polarity distinct from positive and negative electrical charge.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a statement matching the recorded alignment at cooling or the explicit claim about the youngest rocks.

choices.text: In the youngest basalt, they are aligned with the earth's current polarity.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 3 explicitly says the youngest rocks all have normal polarity. Paragraph 1 defines normal polarity as the same polarity as Earths present magnetic field. Those two statements directly support the answer without estimating reversal frequency or invoking modern eruptions.

choices.text: In magma, most but not all of them align themselves with the earth's magnetic field.
choices.explanation: As far as we know, "grains of magnetite (all of them) behave like little compass needles, aligning with the earth's magnetic field".

choices.text: They are not found in other types of rock besides basalt.
choices.explanation: The only rock *mentioned* that has magnetite in it is basalt, but that doesn't establish that basalt is the only rock with magnetite in it.

choices.text: They are about the size of typical grains of sand.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the two sentences we have about magnetite grains reveals the size of these grains.

We couldn't compare them to typical grains of sand.

This answer seems to just want people to think "a grain of this = a grain of that".

choices.text: They are too small to be visible to the naked eye.
choices.tag: Too Strong: too small to see
choices.explanation: Nothing in the two sentences we have about magnetite grains reveals the size of these grains. We have no idea whether they're visible to the naked eye or not.

questions.prompt: If the time intervals between the earth's magnetic field reversals fluctuate greatly, then, based on the passage, which one of the following is most likely to be true?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What were we ever told in the passage about reversals of the magnetic field?

We know from the 1st paragraph that basalt contains some telltale magnetite that signals what the polarity of the magnetic field was at the time it cooled from liquid to solid basalt. So fluctuating intervals (it's positive for a million years, then negative for only 50,000, then positive for 2 million, then negative for 10 million, etc.) could mean that the distribution of up-needles and down-needles from different eras might not be that well balanced. If the magnetic field sometimes stays at one polarity for a really long time, there will be a lot of basalt to match that era. If the field then switches to the other polarity, but just for a short interval, there won't be as much basalt that matches that era.

We know from the 2nd paragraph that on both sides of the mid-ocean ridge are *Alternating stripes of rock with differing polarities laid out in rows*.

Each stripe represents a flip of the magnetic field from one polarity to the other, so if the intervals between polarity switching fluctuates a lot, the stripes will ****not**** be uniform size. If the polarity changed at a constant interval, then the stripes would come out in a regular pattern.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something playing off the relationship between the magnetic field and the polarity of basalt or the striping pattern around the mid-ocean ridge.

choices.text: Compass readings are most likely to be distorted near the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge.
choices.explanation: The youngest rocks near the ridge have normal polarity, but the passage does not establish where compass distortion is most likely or that normal-polarity basalt cannot distort a reading. Variable reversal intervals instead predict unequal stripe widths.

choices.text: It is this fluctuation that causes the ridge to wind around the earth like the seams on a baseball.
choices.explanation:
This is just a Word Salad (smushing together different terms from the passage). There's nothing in the passage connecting magnetic field to the topographical ridge line of the mid-ocean ridge.

Ridge lines of mountains are caused by volcanos and tectonic plates and stuff like that, not by magnetism.

choices.text: Some of the magnetic stripes of basalt on the ocean floor are much wider than others.
choices.explanation:
This is very easy to support language, because the alternative is that "all the stripes of basalt are roughly the same size".

The stripes of basalt are a combination of two factors, *current polarity of Earth + how much ocean floor spreads during that period*.

If the ocean floor spreads 30m while the polarity is positive, then there will be a 30m stripe of positive basalt.

We are told that the ocean floor seems to spread at a pretty constant rate (several cm per year), so a shorter interval at positive polarity will mean a thinner stripe of positive basalt. A long interval at negative polarity will create a fat stripe of negative basalt.

Thus, if the polarity intervals fluctuate a lot (but the ocean-floor spreading goes at a constant rate), you'll get stripes of different sizes .

choices.text: Continental rock is a more reliable indicator of the earth's magnetic field reversals than is oceanic rock.
choices.explanation: We have no way to relate the magnetic field to a comparison between continental and oceanic rock. As far as we know, rock is rock. If it has magnetite in it, then when it cooled into solid form (whether on land or in sea), then it locked in its compass needle.

choices.text: Within any given magnetic stripe on the ocean floor, the age of the basalt does not vary.
choices.explanation:
First of all, this has no connection to the question stem. In fact, the question stem is emphasizing fluctuates greatly, which means *much variation*.

So it's counterintuitive that we would then predict lack of variance. Moreover, if the Earth is at positive polarity for 100,000 years, then all the basalt that came out of the mid-ocean ridge during that period will be in the same stripe on the ocean floor.

If we pick up on rock from that stripe, it might be 50,000 years old, and if we pick up another one, it might be 150,000 years old. Can we say "the age does not vary"?

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would, if true, most help to support the ocean floor spreading theory?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The ocean floor spreading theory is the idea that there are structurally weak zones where the ocean floor is being pulled apart.

As it's pulled apart, magma is able to spurt out of the cracks. It cools and settles into new crust, and as that process repeats, you get a big pile of crust near the crack zone, which is an underwater mountain range named the global mid-ocean ridge.

If we assign the rate of ocean floor spreading a constant rate of around a few cm every year. Then the stripes of alternating polarity match very well with the periods of alternating polarity of the Earth's magnetic field.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Find anything that makes the existing evidence stronger, or that adds new evidence in favor of ocean spreading.

choices.text: There are types of rock other than basalt that are known to distort compass readings.
choices.explanation: The existence of other rocks that have magnetite or some other magnetic component has nothing specific to do with the ocean-spreading theory.

choices.text: The ages of the earth's magnetic reversals have been verified by means other than examining magnetite grains in rock.
choices.explanation: The correlation depends on the assigned dates of magnetic reversals. Independent verification of those dates makes the correlation more trustworthy and therefore strengthens its support for spreading. Strengthening can reinforce the reliability of a premise; it need not supply a wholly new kind of evidence or settle the theory beyond doubt.

choices.text: Pieces of basalt similar to the type found on the mid-ocean ridge have been found on the continents.
choices.explanation:
The ocean-spreading theory doesn't really care if there is basalt on land as well or only in the ocean.

The only relevance of basalt is that it gives off magnetic patterns, and the magnetic patterns near the mid-ocean ridge seem to line up with reversals in earth's magnetic polarity.

choices.text: Along its length, the peak of the mid-ocean ridge varies greatly in height above the ocean floor.
choices.explanation:
The ocean-floor spreading theory doesn't really make any predictions about whether ridge height would vary greatly or only slightly.

Every mountain range on earth varies greatly in terms of height above sea level, so we'd expect an underwater mountain range to vary greatly as well (whether that mountain range was still currently changing or pretty much settled in place).

You know mountains -- they love their peaks and valleys, which vary greatly in height.

choices.text: Basalt is the only type of volcanic rock found in portions of the ocean floor nearest to the continents.
choices.explanation:
The ocean-spreading theory doesn't really care where on Earth there is or isn't basalt. It doesn't care whether near the continents there are portions of only-basalt, or whether basalt is always mixed in rather evenly.

The only relevance of basalt to this theory is that it gives off magnetic patterns, and the magnetic patterns it gives off near the mid-ocean ridge seem to line up with reversals in earth's magnetic polarity.

Whatever basalt is doing on the continents, in (C), or near the continents, in this answer, doesn't really have anything to do with analyzing the *mid-ocean* ridge and interpreting whether it's fixed or spreading.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's no way to pre-game this, we just want to think that the correct answer will be an obnoxious rephrasing of something in the passage, a true statement you can basically derive from some claim in the passage, or a gist-y synthesis of multiple claims.

The wrong answers will say stuff that's Too Strong, an Unknown Comparison, or Unmentioned in the passage.

choices.text: Submarine basalt found near the continents is likely to be some of the oldest rock on the ocean floor.
choices.explanation:
We can support this with the end of the 2nd paragraph and beginning of the 3rd paragraph. The *mid-ocean* ridge, which is the part of the ocean floor ****farthest**** from the continents is where the *new* magma comes out.

That's why ... *at or near the ridge crest (in the middle of the ocean), the rocks are very young, and* *****they become progressively older***** *away from the crest (headed towards the nearest continent).*

So since we know the middle of the ocean is where the newest rock on the ocean floor comes from and since we know that the rocks get progressively older as you move toward the continents, we know that the basalt rocks near the continents are way older than the ones in the middle of the ocean.

We don't necessarily know that basalt rocks are older than other types of rocks, but the language of this answer choice is hedged a bit to allow for that (plus, it's only a Most Supported task). It's just saying "they're likely to be *some of the oldest* rocks".

choices.text: The older a sample of basalt is, the more times it has reversed its polarity.
choices.explanation: Once basalt cools from its liquid molten form to its rock form, the magnetite needles freeze in place. That's the only "polarity" we could speak of a sample of basalt having. So all basalt only has one polarity that's locked in when it cools. It never reverses.

choices.text: Compass readings are more likely to become distorted at sea than on land.
choices.explanation: We don't have any way to compare the magnetic disturbances of the basalt in the ocean to potential magnetic disturbances of basalt (or other magnetic stuff) on land.

choices.text: The magnetic fields surrounding magnetite grains gradually weaken over millions of years on the ocean floor.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: magnetic fields weaken
choices.explanation: Nothing in the passage ever talked about the magnetic field of anything weakening over time, only the magnetic field of earth periodically reversing polarity.

choices.text: Any rock that exhibits present-day magnetic polarity was formed after the latest reversal of the earth's magnetic field.
choices.explanation: Polarity has reversed more than once, and the ocean floor alternates between stripes with normal and reversed polarity. An older stripe can therefore match the present field as well. Matching current polarity does not uniquely identify formation after the latest reversal; the answer confuses a recurring condition with a unique timestamp.

passages.title: Historical Objectivity
passages.text:
**Passage A**

Central to the historian’s profession and scholarship has been the ideal of objectivity. The assumptions upon which this ideal rests include a commitment to the reality of the past, a sharp separation between fact and value, and above all, a distinction between history and fiction.

According to this ideal, historical facts are prior to and independent of interpretation: the value of an interpretation should be judged by how well it accounts for the facts; if an interpretation is contradicted by facts, it should be abandoned. The fact that successive generations of historians have ascribed different meanings to past events does not mean, as relativist historians claim, that the events themselves lack fixed or absolute meanings.

Objective historians see their role as that of a neutral judge, one who must never become an advocate or, worse, propagandist. Their conclusions should display the judicial qualities of balance and evenhandedness. As with the judiciary, these qualities require insulation from political considerations, and avoidance of partisanship or bias. Thus objective historians must purge themselves of external loyalties; their primary allegiance is to objective historical truth and to colleagues who share a commitment to its discovery.

**Passage B**

The very possibility of historical scholarship as an enterprise distinct from propaganda requires of its practitioners that self-discipline that enables them to do such things as abandon wishful thinking, assimilate bad news, and discard pleasing interpretations that fail elementary tests of evidence and logic.

Yet objectivity, for the historian, should not be confused with neutrality. Objectivity is perfectly compatible with strong political commitment. The objective thinker does not value detachment as an end in itself but only as an indispensable means of achieving deeper understanding. In historical scholarship, the ideal of objectivity is most compellingly embodied in the *powerful argument*—one that reveals by its every twist and turn its respectful appreciation of the alternative arguments it rejects. Such a text attains power precisely because its author has managed to suspend momentarily his or her own perceptions so as to anticipate and take into account objections and alternative constructions—not those of straw men, but those that truly issue from the rival’s position, understood as sensitively and stated as eloquently as the rival could desire. To mount a telling attack on a position, one must first inhabit it. Those so habituated to their customary intellectual abode that they cannot even explore others can never be persuasive to anyone but fellow habitués.

Such arguments are often more faithful to the complexity of historical interpretation—more faithful even to the irreducible plurality of human perspectives—than texts that abjure position-taking altogether. The powerful argument is the highest fruit of the kind of thinking I would call objective, and in it neutrality plays no part. Authentic objectivity bears no resemblance to the television newscaster’s mechanical gesture of allocating the same number of seconds to both sides of a question, editorially splitting the difference between them, irrespective of their perceived merits.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The ideal of objectivity in historical scholarship—what it means and how historians should embody it.

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

The two passages present different perspectives on the nature and requirements of objectivity for historians: Passage A describes traditional objectivity as neutrality, detachment, and insulation from bias, while Passage B criticizes equating objectivity with neutrality and argues that genuine objectivity involves strong, well-argued positions that fully consider opposing viewpoints. - The "Most Valuable Sentence" in Passage A is: “Objective historians see their role as that of a neutral judge, one who must never become an advocate or, worse, propagandist.” (P3) - The "Most Valuable Sentence" in Passage B is: “Objectivity is perfectly compatible with strong political commitment. The objective thinker does not value detachment as an end in itself but only as an indispensable means of achieving deeper understanding.” (P2)

**P1 (A): Foundations of the Objectivity Ideal**

Here the author describes traditional beliefs about historical objectivity: historians are supposed to stay committed to what really happened in the past, keep fact separate from value judgments, and keep history distinct from fiction.

**P2 (A): Facts vs. Interpretation**

The passage expands on the ideal: facts should come before any interpretation, and if an interpretation doesn’t fit the facts, it should be ditched. Just because historians disagree about interpretations doesn’t mean the facts themselves are up for grabs.

**P3 (A): Historian as Neutral Judge**

This paragraph says objective historians should act like neutral judges—no advocacy, no propaganda, no bias, and no political involvement. Their main loyalty should be to historical truth and to others who value that same truth.

**P1 (B): Objectivity Requires Self-Discipline**

Objectivity is described as something that requires historians to discipline themselves, reject wishful thinking, and avoid sticking to interpretations that don’t pass basic tests of evidence or logic.

**P2 (B): Commitment vs. Neutrality**

Here, the author pushes back on the traditional view, insisting that objectivity doesn’t mean lacking passion or political commitment. Instead, it’s about crafting strong, persuasive arguments that fairly and deeply engage with opposing viewpoints—true objectivity comes from deeply understanding rival positions, not from simply staying neutral.

**P3 (B): Powerful Argument is True Objectivity**

Real objectivity, the author contends, isn’t about mechanically splitting the difference between sides. It’s about making complex, fair arguments that acknowledge the reality of multiple perspectives, rather than pretending to be “neutral” for neutrality’s sake.

questions.prompt: Both passages are concerned with answering which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
If we focus on just Passage A, it seems like she was trying to answer the question of, "What is this *ideal of objectivity* that historians worry about?", because she spends the rest of the passage answer that question.

If we feel confident about this author's central question, then we could head to the answers and use this stubborn sense of what we want to hear to get us down to 1 or 2 choices.

(We could have alternatively done this with just Passage B's central question)

Passage B also talks about objectivity, for historians, in its best form ("authentic objectivity" / "the highest fruit of the kind of thinking I would call objective").

So we'd expect the correct answer to center around "ideal / optimal practices for historians, when it comes to objectivity".

choices.text: What are the most serious flaws found in recent historical scholarship?
choices.explanation: If it's not talking about "objectivity", then we're definitely not talking to it.

choices.text: What must historians do in order to avoid bias in their scholarship?
choices.explanation:
This answer is trying to be sneaky by encoding our main character, "objectivity", by one of its code names: "avoiding bias".

Bias indicates subjectivity. Being bias-free is synonymous with being objective.

So we can read this answer as, "What must historians do in order to remain objective in their scholarship?"

That's definitely our best available match for "ideal / best practices for historians when it comes to objectivity".

choices.text: How did the ideal of objectivity first develop?
choices.explanation:
This answer choice is baiting us in by being the only one to wave the flag of the magic word, "objectivity".

But neither passage discussed **the origin story** of the ideal of objectivity. We have no idea if the ideal is 100 years old or 1000 years old.

choices.text: Is the scholarship produced by relativist historians sound?
choices.explanation:
The central topic of both passages was "objectivity", which this answer fails to mention.

"Relativist historians" were never discussed in Passage B and are brought up once as a total aside in Passage A.

choices.text: Why do the prevailing interpretations of past events change from one era to the next?
choices.explanation:
The central topic of both passages was how historians think about the ideal of 'objectivity'.

Neither passage talked about "prevailing interpretations" or tried to solve the causal mystery behind why they change as time goes on.

questions.prompt: Both passages identify which one of the following as a requirement for historical research?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The cool thing about the way this question is posed is that if we find a requirement for historical research in one passage, that might be enough to get the right answer! (Unless multiple requirements are listed, and there's only one that overlaps both passages)

If we do a quick CTRL + F for "research", nothing comes up. Neither passage uses that term.

So we should probably interpret the question stem as asking us what's required to be "a historian". Presumably, historians do research.

Passage A starts out of the gate by saying that "the ideal of objectivity" is *central* to the historian's profession and scholarship (i.e. "research").

Does something being "central" mean the same as "a requirement"? Not in super technical way, but in this context it feels pretty allowable to equate those.

Passage A also says in its final paragraph that objective historians cannot become an advocate or propagandist. Their balanced, evenhanded conclusions **require** insulation from political considerations, and avoidance of partisanship or bias.

Okay, so Passage A has said that historians need stuff like
- objectivity
- avoid propaganda
- insulate from political considerations / partisanship / bias

Does Passage B echo any of those?

It definitely talks about objectivity, although it seems to define objectivity in a very different way.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Okay, it's not looking too easy to scan for an overlapping requirement. We should probably head to the answers and work backwards from them, so see if we can find support in both passages.

choices.text: the historian's willingness to borrow methods of analysis from other disciplines when evaluating evidence
choices.explanation: Neither passage talked about borrowing methods of analysis from other disciplines (like from physics, or philosophy, or sociology, etc.).

choices.text: the historian's willingness to employ methodologies favored by proponents of competing views when evaluating evidence
choices.explanation:
Neither passage ever talked about employing a competing views' *methodologies*.

Passage B was big on the idea of inhabiting the arguments of competing views, giving them their most charitable consideration before ultimately disagreeing with them. But even there the author of B never says that a historian needs to adopt someone else's *methodology.*

choices.text: the historian's willingness to relinquish favored interpretations in light of the discovery of facts inconsistent with them
choices.explanation:
The first sentence of Passage B is good support for this:

*The very possibility of historical scholarship **requires** them to do such things as abandon wishful thinking, assimilate bad news, and discard pleasing interpretations that fail elementary tests of evidence and logic.*

"Discarding pleasing interpretations" is a great match for "relinquishing favored interpretations".

The best match from Passage A is probably in the 2nd paragraph:

*if an interpretation is contradicted by the facts, it should be abandoned*.

"An interpretation contradicted by facts" is a good match for "facts inconsistent with an interpretation".

There isn't anything in Passage A that matches up well with "favored interpretations", but this rule being given in the 2nd paragraph would apply to *any* interpretation that conflicts with the facts. And more broadly the author of A was saying that objective historians shouldn't have partisanship / bias / external loyalties, all of which sound like favoring certain interpretations.

choices.text: the historian's willingness to answer in detail all possible objections that might be made against his or her interpretation
choices.tag: Too Strong: in detail, all objections
choices.explanation:
Neither passage says that a historian must be willing to answer *in detail* **all** possible objections.

Passage B definitely talks about giving opposing views a fair hearing, but it never says that a historian has to be willing to give *detailed* responses to **100%** of possible objections. That's a really tall order. Some possible objections might be silly / trivial / bad faith. Does a historian really have to be willing to answer all those in detail?

But even if we could live with Passage B's support for this idea, Passage A doesn't have anything resembling responding to objections in great detail.

choices.text: the historian's willingness to accord respectful consideration to rival interpretations
choices.explanation:
This feels pretty well grounded in Passage B's discussion of the powerful argument -- a historian is supposed to respectfully consider and give fair hearing to rival interpretations.

But there's nothing in Passage A about *rival interpretations* or what a historian is required to do with them.

questions.prompt: The author of passage B and the kind of objective historian described in passage A would be most likely to disagree over whether

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Where do Passage A and Passage B disagree?

Passage A defines objectivity (3rd paragraph) as the "role of a neutral judge", whereas Passage B says at the beginning of its 2nd paragraph that "Objectivity should not be confused with neutrality".

B thinks it's okay to have a political commitment and an opinion, as long as you've respectfully talked through the opposing position.

Passage A says in its 3rd paragraph that objectivity requires "insulation from political considerations and avoidance of partisanship or bias".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Look for something about objectivity --- should it be neutral and apolitical, or can it be opinionated and politically motivated?

But be flexible if the answer seems to be about something else.

choices.text: detachment aids the historian in achieving an objective view of past events
choices.explanation:
It's pretty clear that Passage A would agree with this, but it doesn't seem like we could easily support Passage B saying, "Detachment ****is of no help**** to historians trying to objectively view the past".

Passage B doesn't need his objectivity to be totally neutral, but there still might be moments where detachment can aid a historian. He talks about historians managing "to suspend momentarily his or her own perceptions so as to anticipate and take into account objections and alternate constructions", which sounds like a form of detachment.

choices.text: an objective historical account can include a strong political commitment
choices.explanation:
Passage B has the Agree position. 2nd sentence of the 2nd paragraph:
*Objectivity is perfectly compatible with strong political commitment*.

Passage A has the Disagree position, "objectivity cannot include a strong political commitment". 3rd sentence of the 3rd paragraph:
*[Objective historians should display qualities that] require insulation from political considerations, and avoidance of partisanship or bias*.

choices.text: historians today are less objective than they were previously
choices.explanation:
Neither author discusses whether objectivity is growing or shrinking among historians today.

Both passages are sort of a timeless discussion of what objectivity means.

choices.text: propaganda is an essential tool of historical scholarship
choices.explanation:
Both authors would disagree with this. They both think propaganda is to be avoided.

Passage A explicitly disagrees with this in the beginning of the 3rd paragraph:
*Objective historians ... must never become an advocate or, worse, propagandist.*

Passage B's first sentence suggests that historical scholarship is trying to be distinct from propaganda.

No matter what, Passage B can't be said to *agree* with this answer. We wouldn't find any in B to support the very strong notion that "Propaganda is ****essential****".

choices.text: historians of different eras have arrived at differing interpretations of the same historical events
choices.explanation: A explicitly acknowledges that successive generations have ascribed different meanings to past events. B emphasizes multiple perspectives and rival interpretations. There is no support for treating either as denying that historians have interpreted events differently; we need not make a claim about what everyone in the world believes.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes an attitude toward objectivity present in each passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Passage A doesn't seem to directly indicate her attitude towards objectivity, but her overall tone seems very respectful.

She portrays historians' sense of objectivity in a way that most of us would read positively. She also seems to have the attitude that objectivity is possible, because she counters the view of relativist historians who would that that events lack fixed or absolute (i.e. objective) meanings.

Passage B also seems to like objectivity and consider it an ideal worthy of aspiring to.

Overall, there's weak supporting text in both passages when it comes to the author expressing an attitude towards the concept of "objectivity" in general.

We know that Passage A and Passage B define "objectivity" differently, but they both seem to think that it's something historians should strive to accomplish.

choices.text: Objectivity is a goal that few historians can claim to achieve.
choices.explanation:
Neither passage comments on how successful historians are at achieving this goal of objectivity.

We can't support this strong idea that "most historians don't manage to be objective".

choices.text: Objectivity is essential to the practice of historical scholarship.
choices.explanation:
This seems to be the closest match for what we were looking for: *both authors think that objectivity is a worthy goal for historians to strive for.*

The word "essential" is really strong, but if it's the guiding principle of their work, then we can reasonably assume the authors think it's essential.

Passage A's first line:
***Central to** the historian's profession and scholarship has been the ideal of objectivity.*

Passage B's first line:
*The very possibility of historical scholarship .. **requires** of its practitioners [stuff that's synonymous with objectivity].*

We can tell that the rest of that sentence refers to objectivity because the following sentence says, "Yet objectivity, for the historian, should not be confused with neutrality". This implies that we were just talking about objectivity.

choices.text: Objectivity cannot be achieved unless historians set aside political allegiances.
choices.explanation:
Passage A defines objectivity as casting aside personal opinions and political affiliations.

Passage B does not. Passage B is saying, "you don't have to be neutral to be objective. You can keep your political allegiances. You just have to make a really powerful argument that is super respectful of opposing views and presents them in their most charitable light."

choices.text: Historians are not good judges of their own objectivity.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: not good judges
choices.explanation:
Neither passage has any moment where its author says that historians are bad at judging their own objectivity.

Even though it's reasonable to think that it's hard to judge your own objectivity, there's no textual support to back this up.

choices.text: Historians who value objectivity are becoming less common.
choices.explanation: Neither passage speaks to any emerging trend among historians, and comparison between how much they used to value objectivity and how much they currently do.

questions.prompt: Both passages mention propaganda primarily in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is a Local Purpose question (in order to / serves to / primarily to), so the correct answer is usually reinforcing the setup claim *right* *****before***** the detail we’re being asked about.

In Passage A, the setup claim is that “objective historians see their role as that of a neutral judge, one who must never become an advocate or, worse, propagandist”.

So this author is bringing up *propaganda* to identify is as the antithesis of the objective historian’s goal.

In passage B, there’s less setup, since *propaganda* is mentioned in the very first sentence, but it’s again being used as a foil for historical scholarship.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Both authors are trying to clarify that objective history is ****not**** supposed to be doing propaganda.

choices.text: refute a claim made by proponents of a rival approach to historical scholarship
choices.explanation: Neither passage is combating proponents. They are just talking to us, the reader, explaining that history isn’t supposed to be propaganda.

choices.text: suggest that scholars in fields other than history tend to be more biased than historians
choices.explanation: Neither of the references to propaganda has anything to do with *scholars* in other fields. Both authors would presumably think that a propagandist is not a scholar (or at least when they’re doing propaganda, they’re not doing scholarly work).

choices.text: point to a type of scholarship that has recently been discredited
choices.explanation: The sentences that say propaganda are simply saying, “Historians don’t want to be guilty of propaganda (i.e. brainwashing people with a certain dubious narrative)”. There isn’t any reference to recent scholarship that has been discredited.

choices.text: identify one extreme to which historians may tend
choices.explanation:
This is a weird correct answer. We wanted something like, "identify what history is ****not**** supposed to be". In the sense that this is calling propaganda an extreme version of history (extremes are usually bad), we can kind of see what we wanted here.

This answer makes it sounds as though propaganda lies on the same continuum as more serious, respectable history.

The way Passage A says that "objective historians see their role as ... one who must never ****become**** an advocate, or worse propagandist" does seem to place history on a slippery slope that leads towards advocacy and then propaganda.

You go from just trying to report on what happened, to then trying to suggest to people (advocate) how to think about what happened, to then trying to advance an artificial narrative (propaganda) that is a totally unfair reflection of reality.

The way Passage B says "the very ****possibility**** of historical scholarship as an enterprise ****distinct from**** propaganda requires X". That phrasing suggests that historical scholarship and propaganda are in danger of being the same enterprise.

To even possibly de-couple them, you need to be able to abandon wishful thinking, assimilate bad news, and resist pleasing interpretations that aren't really well supported or reasoned.

So both authors are referring to propaganda as a potential danger that historians can slip into if they're not careful .... or *an extreme* to which they may tend if they don't stay true to the objective history goal.

choices.text: draw contrasts with other kinds of persuasive writing
choices.explanation:
What we were looking for was “the author brought up propaganda to clarify that historians are ****not**** trying to write propaganda”, so this answer is conveying that idea of contrasting propaganda with actual history writing.

Is history writing *persuasive* writing, though? Well, according to Passage B it is. That author is clarifying for us that history writing isn’t neutral. It argues a point of view, but it attains its objectivity by fairly and sensitively considering opposing points of view.

But Passage A doesn’t seem to argue that history is persuasive writing. In fact, Passage A is stressing utter objectivity and neutrality. It should be like a judge's ruling, which we do no think of as "persuasive writing".

Passage A *does* contrast propaganda with advocacy, and advocacy is definitely a form of persuasive writing, but the reason Passage A brought up propaganda was not to contrast it with advocacy (but rather to say that the historian is trying to avoid being a propagandist).

questions.prompt: The argument described in passage A and the argument made by the author of passage B are both advanced by

choices.text: citing historical scholarship that fails to achieve objectivity
showing how certain recent developments in historical scholarship have undermined the credibility of the profession
summarizing opposing arguments in order to point out their flaws
suggesting that historians should adopt standards used by professionals in certain other fields
identifying what are seen as obstacles to achieving objectivity
